title: Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k
description: Walks through finding the longest subarray summing to k, from an O(n squared) brute force scan to an O(n) prefix sum and earliest-index hash map solution.

content.title: Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the maximum length of a contiguous subarray that sums to exactly k. If no such subarray exists, return 0.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose elements sum to exactly k. If there is no such subarray, the answer is 0.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Longest Hiking Stretch With an Exact Net Elevation Change
blocks.text: Think of nums as a log of daily elevation changes on a hike. Walking from the very first day a particular running elevation total was ever seen up to the current day gives the longest stretch whose net change works out to exactly k feet, so it pays to remember only the earliest day each running total was seen, never a later one.

blocks.caption: Longest stretch anchored to the earliest matching running total

blocks.text: No contiguous subarray of nums sums to exactly 7 (the possible sums are 1, 3, 6, 2, 5, and 3), so the answer is 0, confirming why the map must actually be checked for a match rather than assumed to exist.
It helps to ask why a sliding window, which works well on an all positive version of this problem, breaks down here, and what has to change to still answer in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If every value in nums were guaranteed non negative, a sliding window that grows to include more elements and shrinks from the left whenever the sum overshoots k would work, since the running sum only ever moves in one direction as the window changes.

Observation 2: Because negative numbers are allowed, growing the window does not always increase the sum and shrinking it does not always decrease it, so a sliding window has no reliable way to decide which side to move, ruling it out entirely.

Observation 3: The sum of a subarray from index i + 1 to j equals the prefix sum up to j minus the prefix sum up to i, so a subarray summing to k ending at j exists whenever some earlier prefix sum equals the current prefix sum minus k, exactly the kind of lookup a hash map answers in constant time.

Observation 4: Since the goal is the maximum length, and not just whether a match exists or how many matches exist, the map should store only the earliest index at which each prefix sum value was first seen; the earliest start always yields the longest subarray for that prefix sum value, confirmed by tracing nums = [1, -1, 5, -2, 3] with k = 3, where the seeded prefix sum 0 at index -1 is exactly what produces the maximum length of 4.

Recognizing a subarray sum as the difference between two prefix sums, and keeping only the earliest index for each prefix sum value, is what turns this into a single pass, constant time lookup per position while still handling negative numbers correctly.
Check every contiguous subarray directly, keeping a running sum as the subarray grows from each starting index, and track the longest length seen whenever that running sum equals k.

items: Initialize maxLen to 0.
For each starting index i from 0 to n - 1, reset a running sum to 0.
For each ending index j from i to n - 1, add nums[j] to the running sum.
Whenever the running sum equals k, update maxLen to the larger of maxLen and j - i + 1.
After checking every pair of start and end indices, return maxLen.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Restarting the running sum at each new starting index, instead of recomputing a sum from scratch for every pair, keeps this at O(n squared) time rather than O(n cubed).
Using j - i + 1 for the length, updated only when the running sum exactly equals k, correctly tracks the longest matching subarray instead of just detecting whether one exists.
No early exit is applied, since a longer matching subarray could still appear later even after an earlier match has already been found.

blocks.text: Every contiguous subarray is directly summed and compared against k, so the longest subarray that sums to k is guaranteed to be found, regardless of any negative values in nums.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time Complexity: O(n squared), since every pair of start and end indices is examined. Space Complexity: O(1), since only a running sum and the best length seen so far are stored.

Limitation: this approach re-examines overlapping subarrays from scratch for every starting index, without reusing any of the running sum work already done for earlier starting indices, which becomes wasteful once n grows large.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
The brute force wastes effort by restarting the running sum at every new starting index, even though the running total up to any index has already been computed once during an earlier pass.

The key insight is that the sum of nums from index i + 1 to j is just the prefix sum up to j minus the prefix sum up to i, so instead of recomputing sums, a single forward pass can compute the prefix sum once at each index and ask a hash map whether prefix sum minus k has been seen before.

Because the goal is the maximum length rather than a count, the map must store the earliest index each prefix sum value was first seen, since reusing that earliest index, rather than the most recent one, always produces the longest possible subarray for a given prefix sum minus k value.
This turns an O(n squared) nested scan into a single O(n) pass, with the hash map trading a small amount of extra space for a constant time lookup at every position.

Keep a hash map from prefix sum value to the earliest index at which it occurred, seeded with prefix sum 0 at index -1 to correctly capture subarrays that start at index 0. For each position, check whether the current prefix sum minus k has been seen before, and if so, measure the length from just after that earliest index up to the current position.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time Complexity: O(n), since each index is processed once with a constant time hash map lookup and insert. Space Complexity: O(n), since the hash map can store up to one entry per distinct prefix sum value.

This works because every subarray summing to k corresponds to two positions whose prefix sums differ by exactly k, and storing only the earliest index for each prefix sum value guarantees that any match found gives the longest possible subarray ending at the current position, since an earlier start can only make a matching subarray longer, never shorter.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens"],"rows":[["Current prefix sum minus k equals a value already in the map","A valid subarray ending at the current index is found; its length is measured from just after the earliest stored index."],["Current prefix sum minus k is not in the map","No subarray ending at the current index sums to k, so the running maximum length is left unchanged."],["Current prefix sum has already been seen before","The existing earliest index is kept as is, since overwriting it with a later index could only shorten future matches."]]}

items: A hash map is seeded with prefix sum 0 mapped to index -1 before the loop begins, so subarrays starting at index 0 are handled without a special case.

At each index, the running prefix sum is updated first, then checked against prefix sum minus k in the map before the current prefix sum is possibly inserted, so the current index is never mistaken for an earlier occurrence of itself.
The map is only updated when the current prefix sum value is not already present, which is exactly what preserves the earliest index guarantee that maximizes subarray length.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute Force","O(n squared)","O(1)","Recomputes a running sum from every starting index; simple but slow for large n."],["Prefix Sum + Hash Map","O(n)","O(n)","Single forward pass; trades hash map space for a constant time lookup per index."]]}

blocks.text: The prefix sum plus earliest-index hash map pattern is the standard technique whenever a problem asks for the longest subarray matching a sum condition, and seeding the map with prefix sum 0 at index -1 is what correctly captures subarrays that start from the very beginning of the array.

items: Overwriting the stored index every time a prefix sum value reappears, instead of keeping only the first index it was ever seen at, which silently shortens the answer.
Forgetting to seed the map with prefix sum 0 at index -1, which causes subarrays starting at index 0 to be missed entirely.
Trying to use a sliding window here, which only works when every value in nums is non negative.

items: Explicitly explain why a sliding window fails once negative numbers are allowed, before introducing the prefix sum plus hash map approach.
Point out the seeded entry for prefix sum 0 at index -1 as the detail that makes subarrays starting at index 0 work correctly.
Contrast this problem with counting subarrays that sum to k, where the map stores counts of occurrences rather than earliest indices.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer emphasizes maximum length rather than count or existence, think prefix sum with a hash map storing the earliest index per value, not the most recent one.

items: How would the solution change if the question asked for the number of subarrays summing to k instead of the longest one?
Could this be solved without extra space if nums were guaranteed to contain only non negative numbers?
How would you extend this to find the maximum length subarray whose sum is at most k rather than exactly k?
Subarray Sum Equals K uses the same prefix sum idea but stores a count of occurrences per prefix sum value instead of the earliest index, since it needs a total count rather than a maximum length.
Contiguous Array relabels 0s as -1 and reduces to finding the longest subarray summing to 0, the same earliest-index hash map technique used here with k fixed at 0.
Two Sum is the two element ancestor of this pattern, turning a paired lookup into an O(1) hash map check instead of a nested scan.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The optimized prefix sum plus hash map approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, compared to O(n squared) time and O(1) space for the brute force nested scan.

items: Pattern: Prefix sum combined with a hash map storing the earliest index at which each prefix sum value occurred.
Core Idea: A subarray from index i + 1 to j sums to k exactly when the prefix sum at i equals the prefix sum at j minus k, so the earliest such i gives the longest subarray.
Time: O(n), a single forward pass with constant time hash map operations at each index.
Space: O(n), for storing up to one entry per distinct prefix sum value.
Most Important Observation: Only the earliest index for each prefix sum value should ever be stored, since overwriting it with a later index can only shorten, never lengthen, a future match.
Interview Difficulty: Intermediate, since the prefix sum idea is common but correctly seeding the map and keeping only the earliest index takes real care to get right.
One-line memory trick: Seed with 0 at -1, store the first time you see each running total, and let the gap between indices be the length.
